description: We are Soteronautas from Salvador, Brazil. In Challenge #10, we built F.A.R.O.L. (Camada Jev): an explainable tactical decision & route-planning system for Mars EVA astronauts. Fusing real NASA data—THEMIS firmness, HiRISE 1m topography, USGS geology, and Perseverance ground-truth—with astronaut voice across a Helmet HUD, Wrist Cuff, and Mission Console, F.A.R.O.L. turns planetary hazards into safe, transparent A* bypasses, ensuring crew survival and scientific mission success
summary:
We developed F.A.R.O.L. (Jev Layer), an explainable, human-in-the-loop tactical decision-support system and autonomous route planner that guides astronauts during extravehicular activities (EVAs) in Jezero Crater on Mars. Designed to overcome the critical 5-to-20-minute Earth-Mars communication delay, the system runs locally on surface hardware, cross-referencing multi-mission NASA datasets—THEMIS thermal inertia for regolith firmness, HiRISE 1m DEM micro-topography, USGS SIM 3464 geology, and Perseverance ground-truth—with spacesuit biometrics and MEDA atmospheric vortex guardrails.

Far beyond a static map, F.A.R.O.L. operates as an active survival co-pilot: it diagnoses hidden sand traps and steep scarps in real time, computing instant, winding A* bedrock bypasses that drastically reduce traverse risk. Guidance is seamlessly distributed across three mission interfaces—an unobscured Helmet HUD, a touch-expandable Wrist Display with full-visor voice confirmation, and a Central Tactical Console featuring an explainable decision tree. By enabling astronauts to accept, decline, or voice-override route shifts on the fly, F.A.R.O.L. ensures true crew autonomy, transparency, and uncompromising safety on the Red Planet."
details:
F.A.R.O.L. Project (Jev Layer): Would an Astronaut Survive a Martian Dust Devil... Without Waiting for Earth?

We are standing on the brink of human exploration on Mars. Between our first steps in Jezero Crater and safe surface missions lies a harsh reality: Earth is up to 24 minutes away by radio. When an astronaut is walking on Mars, waiting for Mission Control isn't an option—it’s a fatal delay. F.A.R.O.L. is more than a navigation map. It is an autonomous, easy-to-understand survival co-pilot built to protect astronauts on the Red Planet.

What is F.A.R.O.L. (Jev Layer)?

F.A.R.O.L. is a local command center for astronauts walking on Mars (EVAs). Instead of relying on Earth, it runs directly on local hardware, dividing Jezero Crater into a smart 20m20m grid. In milliseconds, it combines NASA satellite maps with live data from the Perseverance rover and the astronaut’s spacesuit to guide every step safely.

Features That Define the Future:

Safe Paths Over Hidden Traps

Forget static maps. F.A.R.O.L. uses NASA elevation and heat-retention data to read the Martian ground before the astronaut steps on it. It spots steep slopes (>12) and invisible traps of soft, loose sand. If a path is dangerous, the system immediately blocks that area and calculates a safe detour in real time.

Clear Decisions, Human in Command

In space, astronauts cannot trust a system that hides how it thinks. F.A.R.O.L. uses transparent rules and displays simple, clear reasons on the helmet visor—explaining why a path is blocked or safe. Best of all, the astronaut always has the final say: they can accept or reject alerts using simple voice commands ("JEV, CONFIRM"), and the system instantly adapts to their choice.

Balancing Health and Discovery

Exploration means staying alive while making new discoveries. F.A.R.O.L. watches the astronaut’s oxygen use during steep climbs and suggests slowing down by 20% to prevent exhaustion. At the same time, it uses the Perseverance rover’s sensors to find valuable rocks—authorizing a 3-minute science stop only when the ground and weather are completely safe.

The Decisive Difference: Live Mars Weather & "Field Truth"

This is what sets F.A.R.O.L. apart. It connects directly to Perseverance’s weather station on Mars. If a sudden drop in air pressure warns of an approaching dust storm (Dust Devil), an emergency rule overrides everything and tells the astronaut to stop and anchor immediately. Even better: if the astronaut spots soft sand or a crack that satellites missed, a quick voice note updates the map instantly and warns against similar ground nearby.

Our Mission: Engineering for Autonomy

The next giant leap depends on tools as smart and adaptable as our astronauts. By combining NASA space data, live rover sensors, and human intuition, F.A.R.O.L. answers the one question that matters on Mars: Is the crew safe to take the next step?

Because on another world, survival is just the starting point. We’re engineering for safe, autonomous discovery.
